Systems and Networking, stage 14 of 15Next stage: 15 Data Centers and Power

In plain terms

One AI chip is not enough to train a model. So seventy-two of them are wired together in a rack, a cabinet the size of a wardrobe, and run as one computer. Each chip sits on its own board and draws more than a thousand amps, several times the current a whole house is wired to carry. The chips have to swap results with each other all the time. A copper wire can carry those signals only a few meters before they fade, so the longer links send them as light down glass fiber. Many companies can build the rack, but only a few can make the lasers that send the light.

In short

In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion in the laser maker Lumentum, alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment and rights to future capacity for advanced laser components[21]. Indium phosphide is used in high-speed lasers for optical communications, and China produced 70 percent of the world's indium in 2025[22].

On 4 February 2025 China added indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on, to its export control list[29]. AXT, a US-listed maker of those wafers, does all its manufacturing in China[29]. In its filing for the quarter to June 2026, AXT said it could not estimate when it would resume shipping the wafers to the United States[29].

Why substitution is possible
Rack assembly can be moved, though the move would likely take several quarters, an unsourced estimate. UALink is an open specification for the same job as NVLink, and AMD's Helios rack, launched in July 2026, runs it over Ethernet. Since May 2025 Nvidia's NVLink Fusion program has let other firms' custom chips use NVLink, so the dependence on Nvidia stays.
Where China stands

Chinese firms such as InnoLight assemble high-speed optical modules in volume, at sites including Suzhou and Thailand. In February 2025 China put indium under new export restrictions and began requiring export permits for indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on.

Where the US stands

American firms make the switch chips, the links that join accelerators inside a rack, and the lasers. Nvidia said in August 2026 that Wistron's new plant in Fort Worth, Texas, was producing its GB300 superchips and that Foxconn was building a factory in Houston.

Before a chip package can compute, it has to be built into a machine. Building that machine is a separate industry from making the package.

How it works

An accelerator (the AI chip) ships as a module, the chip on a small board with its power supply and memory stacks. Nvidia calls its version SXM, and the open-standards equivalent is the Open Compute Project's accelerator module. Eight modules bolt onto a baseboard that carries their power and the switch chips, which pass data between any two modules at full speed.

Rack-scale systems drop the baseboard and put the chips on trays stacked in the rack. An Nvidia GB300 NVL72 holds 18 compute trays plus nine switch trays, 72 GPUs in all, and draws up to 142 kW[1]. The newer Vera Rubin NVL72 uses the same rack footprint[2].

Inside the rack the trays reach each other over copper. Between neighboring racks, the signal can travel up to 7 meters over active electrical cables, a type of copper cable sold by firms such as Credo[3]. Longer links run on glass fiber, with an optical transceiver at each end. A laser in the sending transceiver turns the electrical signal into pulses of light, and a detector in the receiving one turns the pulses back into current.

Every AI cluster runs two networks that are not interchangeable. Scale-up connects anywhere from a few dozen accelerators to thousands closely enough that they can read each other's memory. It runs at terabytes per second. Scale-out joins those groups to one another at hundreds of gigabits per second. A byte is eight bits, so scale-up is tens of times faster than scale-out.

A model too big for one accelerator is split across many. The parts that exchange data constantly stay inside the scale-up group, while whole blocks of layers can sit on different groups across the slower scale-out network[4]. So scale-up bandwidth sets how efficiently a large model trains.

Variants and trade-offs

Scale-up: NVLink, UALink and Google's torus

The designs differ in how many accelerators can share one pool of memory.

  • NVLink and NVSwitch. Nvidia's per-GPU bandwidth went from 900 GB/s in NVLink 4 to 1,800 in NVLink 5, and the rack's own network moves 130 TB/s on Blackwell[5]. Nvidia's Rubin launch release of January 2026 gives NVLink 6 as 3,600 GB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s for a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack[6]. As of October 2026, Nvidia's NVLink product page still lists preliminary figures of 3,000 GB/s and 216 TB/s[5].
  • UALink. The open specification runs 200 Gb/s per lane, four lanes to a station for 800 Gb/s, and can address up to 1,024 endpoints in one group[7]. AMD's Helios rack, launched in July 2026, joins 72 GPUs and runs UALink over Ethernet for its scale-up network[8].
  • Google's 3D torus. Google wires 64 of its Ironwood TPU accelerators into each rack, called a cube[9]. Inside the cube each chip links directly to six others, in a three-dimensional grid that Google calls a 3D torus[9]. Optical circuit switches join cubes into superpods of 9,216 chips that can bypass a failed cube or link[9].

Scale-out: InfiniBand versus Ethernet

InfiniBand, the specialized network built for supercomputers, was the main scale-out network when AI clusters were small and uniform. Ethernet switch capacity grew quickly. Broadcom, which sells its switch chips to any buyer, doubled their bandwidth in each generation, from 25.6 Tbps on one chip in Tomahawk 4[10] to 51.2 in Tomahawk 5[11] and 102.4 in Tomahawk 6[12]. In June 2025 the Ultra Ethernet Consortium published its 1.0 specification, a set of Ethernet-based communication protocols for AI and supercomputing that covers transport, congestion control and direct memory access[13].

Nvidia sells both networks. Its data center revenue reached $89.0 billion in the quarter to July 2026, up 117 percent from a year earlier[14]. In the quarter before, it credited its data center growth to Blackwell 300 products and to demand for its "InfiniBand, Spectrum-X Ethernet, and NVLink" solutions[15].

Optics: pluggable, then co-packaged

A cluster needs several transceivers, the modules that turn electricity into light and back, for each accelerator. Their power cost is one reason Broadcom and Nvidia are moving the optics out of pluggable modules and into the switch chip's own package, a design called co-packaged optics. Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 Davisson cuts optical interconnect power by 70 percent, more than 3.5 times lower than traditional pluggable modules[16]. It keeps its lasers in field-replaceable modules[16]. Nvidia's Spectrum-X Photonics switches, due in 2026, reach 512 ports of 800 gigabits and use four times fewer lasers than traditional designs[17].

Who makes it

Optical modules are assembled where labor and land are cheap, and the Chinese makers went offshore early. InnoLight has run a plant in Thailand since 2019, alongside its sites in Suzhou and Taiwan[18]. The Thai subsidiary of Eoptolink, another Chinese module maker, lists sites in Chonburi and Rayong[19].

The Federal Communications Commission publishes a Covered List of equipment and services judged to pose an unacceptable risk to US national security or to the security and safety of US persons[20]. Its July 2026 order bars new authorizations for devices that contain logic-bearing hardware components produced by firms on that list[20]. Commenters in the record named optical transceivers as one such component[20]. The same order notes that the key players in the optical transceiver market, Coherent and InnoLight among them, do not appear on the Covered List[20].

The lasers inside those modules come from far fewer firms. In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion in one of them, Lumentum, alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment and future capacity access rights for advanced laser components[21].

Indium phosphide is used in the high-speed laser diodes and photodetectors for optical communications[22]. China accounted for 70 percent of world indium production in 2025[22]. In February 2025 China's Ministry of Commerce placed indium under new export restrictions[22].

Two US firms, Broadcom and Marvell, design both custom accelerators and switch chips. Broadcom sells the Ethernet switch chips that other firms build their switches around, along with custom AI accelerators. Its AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, up 221 percent from a year earlier[23]. Marvell's five-year agreement with Amazon Web Services, announced in December 2024, covers custom AI chips alongside the optical and networking parts that go with them[24].

Taiwanese firms do much of the physical assembly. Foxconn booked NT$8.1 trillion of revenue in 2025, up 18 percent, with cloud and networking among the drivers[25]. In the same results release, its chairman called Foxconn the world's largest AI server provider[25].

Some assembly is moving to the United States. In April 2025 Nvidia said it was building supercomputer manufacturing plants in Texas, with Foxconn in Houston and Wistron in Dallas[26]. It expected mass production to ramp up in the following 12 to 15 months[26]. In August 2026 Nvidia said Wistron's new plant in Fort Worth, Texas, near Dallas, was producing its GB300 superchips and Foxconn was building its factory in Houston[27].

The chokepoint

Several contract manufacturers on three continents assemble racks. The power shelves, copper busbars, cables and connectors have many suppliers. In its filing for the quarter to April 2026, Nvidia said the complexity of rack-scale systems had caused production delays[15]. Moving Foxconn's share of rack assembly to other assemblers such as Quanta and Wistron would likely take several quarters, though no source puts a figure on it.

Four components that go into the rack take longer to replace.

  • Indium phosphide laser capacity. In March 2026 Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion in Coherent, alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment and future access and capacity rights for Coherent's advanced laser and optical networking products[28].
  • Indium phosphide substrates. China added indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on, to its export control list on 4 February 2025[29]. AXT, a US-listed maker of these wafers, does all its manufacturing in China[29]. In its filing for the quarter to June 2026, AXT called the export permits the most significant challenge it faces[29]. It said it could not estimate when it would resume shipping the wafers to the United States[29].
  • NVSwitch. NVLink and its switch chip, NVSwitch, are Nvidia's own designs. UALink is an open standard designed for accelerator communications within one scale-up group[7]. Since May 2025 Nvidia's NVLink Fusion program has let other firms' custom chips use NVLink, including CPUs from Fujitsu and Qualcomm that connect to Nvidia GPUs[30].
  • High-layer-count circuit boards. The boards, and the low-loss laminate they are built from, are concentrated in Taiwan and Japan. See Substrates and PCBs.

Optical module assembly is concentrated, but firms choose where to do it based on cost and policy. It has moved before, as the Chinese makers' Thai plants show[18].

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

What is an AI rack?

A cabinet of 72 AI chips wired together to run as one computer.

The chips swap results with each other constantly. Reread: How it works

Why do the longer links between AI chips carry signals as light?

Copper carries the signals only a few meters.

Active copper cables carry the signal up to 7 meters between racks. Beyond that a laser turns the signal into pulses of light that travel down glass fiber. Reread: How it works

Which parts of an AI rack are hardest to replace?

Nvidia's NVLink switch chips, which connect the AI chips in a rack, and the lasers for the optical links.

By contrast, rack assembly can move from Foxconn to Quanta or Wistron, though the move would take an estimated several quarters. Reread: The chokepoint

What does China control in the optical links?

About 70 percent of the world's 2025 output of indium, the raw material for the lasers.

Since February 2025 China has required export permits for indium phosphide substrates, the wafers the lasers are grown on. Chinese firms also assemble high-speed optical modules in volume. Reread: The chokepoint
